title: Prompts for selling and talking about what you do
intro: Here are the texts you need to get someone to pay you: the website, the service page, the quote, and what you say on the phone when they ask for the price. Use these once you already know how to do something and what you're missing is talking about it without sounding like a brochure. Copy the prompt, swap out what's in brackets, and paste it into your AI's text box.
model: ChatGPT for everyday use (posts, emails, follow-ups), Claude when the text is long and has to sound like you (the whole website, the quote, the case study), and Gemini if your source material is in a Google Drive document or in a video of yours.

prompts.name: The sentence that explains what you do
prompts.when: Before any other piece of text. If you don't have this sentence, your website, your quote, and your posts will all come out fuzzy.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a copywriter (someone who writes text to sell things) with twenty years writing messages for freelancers and small businesses. Your goal: someone who has never heard of me understands in under five seconds what I do and why they should care.

Details about my business:
- What I do, in my own unpolished words: [WHAT YOU DO]
- Who pays me: [WHO YOU SELL TO]
- The headache I take off that person's plate: [PROBLEM YOU SOLVE]
- What it costs them not to fix it: [WHAT THEY LOSE IF THEY DON'T FIX IT]
- Roughly what I charge: [APPROXIMATE PRICE]
- How I normally talk: [WARM / FORMAL / FUNNY]

Do it like this:
1. Write 10 one-line sentences, 15 words max each, saying what I do, for whom, and what that person gets. "Tailored solutions," "synergies," "strategic partner," and "digital transformation" are banned.
2. Each sentence in a different register: one very direct, one with a number in it, one that opens with the problem, one that compares against what they do today, one written the way one of my clients would say it.
3. Below each sentence, one short line: which kind of client it fits best, and what risk it carries (for instance, overpromising).
4. At the end, pick the 3 best yourself and explain in two sentences why those.
5. Then ask me the 5 questions whose answers would most improve these sentences.

If any detail I gave you is vague or missing, don't make it up: tell me exactly what's missing and keep going with what you have. Reply with only the sentences and their notes, no intro or sign-off.
fill: Your work in the rough, the way you'd tell a friend. Example: "I build small online stores and get them fully running, payment gateway and all"
The specific type of client, not "businesses." Example: "craftspeople who sell at markets and want to sell online too"
The real pain, in their words. Example: "they lose sales because they only take Venmo and have nowhere to send people"
[WHAT THEY LOSE IF THEY DON'T FIX IT]
The measurable consequence. Example: "at every market someone asks ten times if they sell online, and those sales just evaporate"
Your real number. Example: "$1,300 for the store fully built, $45 a month for upkeep"
How you actually talk. Example: "warm, always casual, zero jargon"
prompts.expect: Ten very different sentences, with notes below each, and a list of questions at the end. A couple will make you cringe: that's normal, the value is in the three that survive.
prompts.next: Pick one, read it out loud, and keep the one you can say without blushing. You'll reuse that sentence in every prompt that follows: paste it into the [WHAT YOU DO] field of the others.

prompts.name: Your website's homepage
prompts.when: When you're about to build your website (or fix the one you have) and don't know what to put in each spot.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a website copywriter, and as someone who thinks about what a person sees the moment they land on a page. Write me the full text for my website's homepage. I don't know how to code: whatever you give me I'm going to paste in exactly where it goes, so hand it to me organized with clear labels.

My business: [WHAT YOU DO]
My ideal client: [WHO YOU SELL TO]
What I want a visitor to do: [ACTION YOU WANT]
Proof I have that this works: [PROOF YOU HAVE]
Price or price range: [APPROXIMATE PRICE]

Give it back to me with this exact structure, in this order, with these headings in capital letters so I know where each piece goes:
1. HEADLINE: one line, 12 words max.
2. SUBHEADLINE: two lines explaining how I deliver it.
3. BUTTON: three text options for the main button.
4. WHO IT'S FOR: three bullet points. WHO IT'S NOT FOR: two honest bullet points.
5. HOW WE WORK: three steps, one sentence each.
6. WHAT'S INCLUDED AND WHAT'S NOT: two facing lists.
7. PROOF: where I'd place testimonials and what each one should say to actually matter.
8. PRICE: how to present the number without scaring people off or losing them.
9. FAQ: five questions with a three-line answer each, including the awkward one about price.
10. CLOSING AND FINAL BUTTON.

Rules: short sentences, casual tone, plain everyday English. No "excellence," "comprehensive solutions," or "committed to quality." Mark anything you claim that I can't back up with a fact as [NO PROOF] so I can decide whether to keep it. If you're missing details, still hand me a complete first draft and ask for what's missing at the end, as a list of six questions max.
fill: The sentence you got from the previous prompt. Example: "I build online stores for craftspeople and have them taking payments in two weeks"
Your ideal client in detail. Example: "potters and jewelry makers already selling at markets, making $15,000-60,000 a year"
One single thing. Example: "book a 20-minute call on my calendar" or "message me on WhatsApp"
Whatever is true. Example: "11 stores built, 3 clients who've stuck with me over a year, one that went from $0 to $450 a month". If you have nothing, write "none yet" and the AI will work around it
Your number. Example: "from $900 up to $2,500 depending on the catalog"
prompts.expect: The entire website copy, broken into numbered sections, with some sentences flagged [NO PROOF] and a list of questions at the end.
prompts.next: Remove everything marked [NO PROOF] that you can't back up, and answer the closing questions in the same chat by asking it to "rewrite with this." Only then do you paste it onto your site.

prompts.name: A service page
prompts.when: When someone asks "and what exactly does that include?" and you have to improvise the answer every single time.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a business consultant with years selling professional services. Turn something I do into a service page that sells itself, so I don't have to explain it over the phone every time.

Service: [SERVICE NAME]
What I actually do, step by step: [WHAT YOU DELIVER]
How long it takes: [TIMELINE]
What I need from the client to be able to work: [WHAT THE CLIENT MUST GIVE YOU]
Price: [PRICE]
What people commonly get wrong about this service: [COMMON MISUNDERSTANDING]

Give me back the page with these sections, in this order:
- Service name: three alternatives, none with made-up buzzwords.
- One sentence stating the outcome the client walks away with, not the task I perform.
- Who it's for and at what point in their situation it makes sense to hire it.
- WHAT'S INCLUDED: closed list, each item a concrete, checkable deliverable.
- WHAT'S NOT INCLUDED: honest list, at least four items, starting with the ones that usually cause trouble.
- How it works: four steps with their approximate timing.
- What I need from you: what the client has to provide, and what happens if they don't provide it in time.
- Price and payment terms, with the exact figure, and what happens if the project grows along the way.
- A realistic commitment (no "satisfaction guaranteed" if I'm not actually going to refund).
- Three FAQs with their answers.

Write it addressing the client casually, in plain everyday English, short sentences. Translate any technical term the first time you use it. If the price I gave you doesn't match the work I described, tell me clearly before giving me the page. If information is missing, write [MISSING: whatever it is] inside the text instead of making it up.
fill: What you call it now. Example: "turnkey online store"
Everything you do, out of order if needed. Example: "pick a template, upload up to 30 products, set up card payments, connect shipping, run a one-hour training video call"
Real time, not optimistic. Example: "two weeks from when I get the photos"
Example: "product photos, prices, text for each product, and their bank details"
Example: "$1,300 plus $45 a month for upkeep"
Example: "they think I write the text for each product, and I don't"
prompts.expect: A complete page with the "what's not included" list well filled out, which is the part that prevents mid-project arguments.
prompts.next: Paste it onto your site as the service page and send it ahead of time to anyone who asks about it. If the AI flagged the price as off, sit down and run the numbers before publishing it.

prompts.name: A batch of posts from one idea
prompts.when: When you know you should be posting, you only have one idea in your head, and you don't want to sit down and think it through every day.
prompts.prompt:
Act as the content lead for a small account selling professional services. Write me a batch of posts for [SOCIAL NETWORK] built from a single idea, so I don't have to decide what to post every morning.

Idea or thing that happened to me: [IDEA OR EXPERIENCE]
What I sell: [WHAT YOU DO]
Who I want it to reach: [WHO YOU SELL TO]
What I want to achieve: [GOAL]

Give me 10 different posts. For each one:
- An opening line that stops the scroll, no empty clickbait or hollow rhetorical questions.
- The full body text, ready to copy and paste, at the length that works for that platform.
- A closing line inviting a reply or a message, different in each post.
- In parentheses, what photo or screenshot would go with it.

Split the 10 like this: 3 telling a story about something I did and how it went (including what went wrong), 2 explaining a common mistake people in my field make, 2 answering a question I get asked a lot, 2 with an opinion someone might disagree with, and 1 talking openly about what I sell and its price.

Write in first person, plain everyday English, short sentences, no emojis unless I tell you otherwise. Banned: "the key is," generic five-tip lists, and any sentence that would work equally well for a plumber as for a lawyer. If the idea I gave you doesn't stretch far enough, tell me and ask for two more concrete examples instead of padding it with filler.
fill: Where you post. Example: "LinkedIn," "Instagram," or "an email newsletter"
Something that really happened to you, the more specific the better. Example: "a client had been paying $100 a month for two years for a site nobody visited"
Your one-line sentence. Example: "I build online stores for craftspeople"
Example: "potters and jewelry makers who sell at markets"
One single thing. Example: "get people to DM me" or "get people to understand this doesn't cost $5,000"
prompts.expect: Ten complete, distinct posts, each with an image idea. Two or three will be good, the rest will give you a starting point.
prompts.next: Rewrite the opening line of each one by hand in your own words: that's what stands out the most. Schedule one every two or three days instead of dropping them all at once.

prompts.name: Script for a sales call
prompts.when: The day before a call with a potential client, so you don't wing it.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a veteran salesperson who sells services over phone and video calls. Prepare me a script for a first call, [DURATION] minutes long, with a potential client. I don't want a word-for-word script: I want to know what to ask, in what order, and what to do when the conversation goes sideways.

Context: I sell [WHAT YOU DO] to [WHO YOU SELL TO], for around [APPROXIMATE PRICE]. This person came in through [WHERE THE CLIENT CAME FROM] and the only thing I know about them is: [WHAT YOU ALREADY KNOW ABOUT THEM].

Structure the call in blocks, with the approximate minute each one starts:
1. Opening, 30 seconds: what I say so they know what this is and how long it'll take.
2. Questions: eight questions ranked from general to specific, that help me understand their problem, their timeline, their budget, and who actually decides. Under each question, what to listen for in the answer and what would be a red flag.
3. Playback: how I summarize out loud what they told me to prove I understood.
4. My spoken proposal: how I lay out in 90 seconds what I'd do, without getting into technical detail.
5. Price: the exact line I use to say the number, without apologizing and without rushing, and what I do right after saying it.
6. Close: how we agree on a next step with a concrete date.
7. Signs this client isn't a good fit, and how I exit the call gracefully.

Add at the end three emergency lines for when my mind goes blank. Plain everyday English, casual tone. If context is missing, assume whatever's most typical for my field and flag that assumption in brackets so I can correct it.
fill: How long it actually runs. Example: "20"
Your one-line sentence. Example: "online stores built and running in two weeks"
How they found you. Example: "one of their clients referred them" or "they filled out the site's form"
Whatever little you know, verbatim if possible. Example: "they wrote: I have a site but can't take payments through it, and I'm swamped"
prompts.expect: A script broken into timed blocks, the eight questions with what to listen for, and the exact line for stating the price.
prompts.next: Print it out or keep it open in a tab during the call. Afterward, go back to the chat, tell it how it went, and ask it to adjust the questions that didn't work.

prompts.name: Response to the price objection
prompts.when: Right when they say "that's expensive," or better yet: the day before, so you have it ready.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a sales trainer. I'm about to hear the price objection and I want the response ready before it lands, not improvised with my pulse racing.

My service: [WHAT YOU DO]
My price: [PRICE]
What the client said, verbatim: [WHAT THE CLIENT SAID]
Who or what they're comparing me to: [COMPETITOR OR ALTERNATIVE]
How far I can move on price or scope without losing money: [YOUR REAL MARGIN]

Give me this:
1. What's really behind that line: four possible translations ("I don't have the money," "I don't see what I get for it," "I'm comparing quotes," "I'm not the one who decides") and a single question that lets me tell which one it is before I respond to anything.
2. Three written responses ready to say out loud, under 60 words each: one for when there's genuinely no budget, one for when they don't see the value, one for when they're comparing me to someone cheaper. None of them can drop the price just because.
3. Two ways to move the deal without touching my rate: cut scope, change the timeline, or change the payment terms, with the exact figure for each option.
4. The line in the sand: at what point I say no, in exactly what words, and how I say it without burning the relationship in case they come back in six months.

Plain everyday English, casual tone, no textbook sales tricks or used-car-salesman lines. If from what I've told you my price is clearly out of line with the market, in either direction, tell me before giving me the responses.
fill: Your service in one line. Example: "I build turnkey online stores"
The figure you quoted them. Example: "$1,300 plus $45 a month"
Copy and paste their line verbatim. Example: "ugh, that seems like a lot, my nephew could do it for $300"
Example: "a nephew, a $20-a-month template, or doing nothing"
Be honest with yourself. Example: "I can go down to $1,000 if I drop the training and the copywriting, below $850 I lose money"
prompts.expect: A read on what their line actually means, three short memorizable responses, and two alternatives with figures.
prompts.next: Memorize the question from point 1 and always use it before responding. Save the three responses in a note on your phone: you'll use them with every client, not just this one.

prompts.name: A written quote
prompts.when: After the call, when it's time to send the proposal and you don't want it to shrink into a three-line email with just a number.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a consultant who prepares business proposals. Write me a written quote the client can understand and accept without calling me to ask what each thing means.

Client: [CLIENT NAME], works in [CLIENT'S FIELD]
What they asked me for, in their words: [WHAT THEY ASKED FOR]
What I think they actually need: [WHAT YOU WOULD DO]
Price and payment terms: [PRICE AND HOW IT'S PAID]
Timeline: [TIMELINE]
How long this offer is valid: [EXPIRATION DATE]

Structure the document like this:
1. One-page summary: what problem we solve, what I deliver, how much it costs, and when it's ready. It has to make sense reading only this.
2. What I understood about their situation, in their own words, so they feel heard.
3. What I'm proposing and why this way, not some other way.
4. Deliverables: numbered list, each with exactly what they get and in what format.
5. Timeline by phase, with dates.
6. What I need from you to hit those dates, and what happens to the timeline if it doesn't arrive in time.
7. Out of scope: what's NOT included, and what it would cost to add it, with the exact figure.
8. Price, payments, and what happens if the project stops or changes midway.
9. Terms: who owns the work once it's finished, how many rounds of revisions are included, and how long the offer stands.
10. Next step: one single clear action.

Plain everyday English, casual tone, no legal jargon, short sentences. Flag with [REVIEW] any point where you're assuming something I haven't told you. Don't invent legal clauses: if you think one is missing, flag it for me to check with someone, but don't write it as if it were valid.
fill: The person's or business's name. Example: "Robles Ceramics"
Example: "a ceramics studio that sells at markets and by custom order"
Copy their words from the email or the call. Example: "I want to take payments through the site without handing out my bank details to people"
Your professional judgment. Example: "a store with 25 products, card payments, shipping via the postal service, and a one-hour training session"
Example: "three weeks from when I receive the photos"
Example: "September 30." Putting a date moves more quotes than nagging does
prompts.expect: A long, well-organized document, with the "out of scope" section filled in and a few [REVIEW] flags where it made assumptions.
prompts.next: Go over every [REVIEW] one by one before sending it: that's where commitments you didn't intend to make slip in. If the amount is large or the work spans months, have a lawyer look over the terms (a basic review runs around $100-200).

prompts.name: Writing up a finished project
prompts.when: When you've wrapped up a project you're proud of and want it to help sell the next one.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a journalist who writes client case studies. Turn a project I've already finished into a story that another, different client reads and thinks "that's exactly what's happening to me."

Client and field: [CLIENT AND FIELD]
What their situation was before: [SITUATION BEFORE]
What they asked me for: [WHAT THEY ASKED FOR]
What I did, in no particular order: [WHAT YOU DID]
What got complicated along the way: [PROBLEM THAT CAME UP]
Result, with numbers if I have them: [RESULT]
What it cost and how long it took: [PRICE AND TIMELINE]
Can I use the client's name?: [YES / NO]

Give me three versions of the same case:
A) Long version for the website, 500-600 words, with these sections: the starting situation, what it was costing them, what we did, the moment it hit a snag and how I solved it, the result, and a client quote you'll mark as [ASK CLIENT FOR QUOTE].
B) Short version for a post, 150 words, told as a story with no self-congratulation.
C) Three-line version to drop into a sales call when someone asks if I've done anything similar.

In all three versions: no superlatives, no percentage or figure I haven't given you, and translate any technical term into what it means for the client's business. If I've told you I can't use their name, write an anonymous description that's still credible (for example, "a two-person ceramics studio in a mid-sized city"). At the end, tell me what detail is missing that would make this case more convincing, and how I could get it.
fill: Example: "they only sold at markets and over WhatsApp, writing orders down in a notebook"
Their words. Example: "a website to sell through, but nothing complicated"
Everything, even if it comes out messy. Example: "a store with 25 products, card payments, automatic shipping labels, one hour of training"
What went sideways. Example: "the photos were taken on a phone against a dirty white wall; they had to be redone". This is the part that makes the case believable
Only what's actually true. Example: "6 orders the first month, $420; now around $780 a month". If you don't have numbers, say so and the AI won't invent them
If you haven't asked the client yet, put NO
prompts.expect: Three versions of the same case, with the client quote flagged as pending, and a list of what detail is still missing.
prompts.next: Get written permission from the client before publishing their name, and ask them for the quote line while they're still happy. Warning: publishing something online has no undo button; even if you take the page down later, screenshots and search engine copies linger.

prompts.name: Following up when there's no answer
prompts.when: Several days have passed since the quote and there's silence. Before writing them off or sending something pushy.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a patient, considerate salesperson. I sent a quote and haven't heard back. Write me the full follow-up sequence so I don't just sit still, and don't come across as pushy either.

What I sent and when: [WHAT YOU SENT AND WHEN]
Price: [PRICE]
The last thing this person said to me: [THE LAST THING THEY SAID]
How we're in touch: [CHANNEL]
How important this client is to me: [A LOT / NORMAL]

Give me four messages, noting the day each one gets sent counting from when I sent the quote:
1. A short reminder that doesn't sound like a reproach or a plea.
2. A message that offers something useful (an idea, a fact, a similar example) with no ask attached.
3. A message that makes it easy for them to say no, with a closed yes-or-no question.
4. A polite close: leave the door open and stop writing.

Each message: 80 words max, with a subject line if it's an email. Banned: "hope you're doing well," "just wanted to check if...", and apologizing for writing. Under each message, tell me what it means if they reply and what it means if they don't.

At the end, tell me what signs mean this client isn't going to buy, and how long it makes sense to wait before letting it go. Plain everyday English, casual tone. If you can't write something specific from the context I gave you, ask me for one more detail instead of padding it with pleasantries.
fill: Example: "the online store quote, Tuesday the 5th, by email"
Verbatim. Example: "let me run it by my partner and I'll get back to you this week"
Be honest: it changes the tone and number of attempts. Example: "a lot, this is exactly the kind of client I want more of"
prompts.expect: Four short messages with their send date, plus a read on what each reply or each silence means.
prompts.next: Put all four dates in your phone's calendar right now, with the message pasted into the reminder note. That's the one thing that actually makes the follow-up happen.

canDo: Translate what you do into words someone outside your field can understand. By far its strongest suit.
Give you ten different versions of the same thing in thirty seconds, so you pick instead of writing from a blank page.
Organize a long document (a quote, a proposal) without forgetting the "what's not included" section, which is where almost every dispute starts.
Prepare you for the uncomfortable moment before it happens: the price objection, the client who goes quiet, the call that goes sideways.
cantDo: It doesn't know if your price is right for your city and your field. If you don't give it your real numbers, it'll invent some with total confidence.
It doesn't know your clients' actual results. If you ask for a case study with no data, it'll hand back fake-looking percentages that seem real: check every one before publishing anything.
It doesn't know your voice. Early drafts will sound like a bank brochure until you paste in a couple of your own texts and say "write like this."

It can't make commitments on your behalf. Guarantees, deadlines, and legal terms are your call, and if the contract is significant, it's worth having a lawyer look it over (a basic review runs around $100-200).
tips: Paste in two or three texts you've written yourself (an email to a client, a WhatsApp message) and say: "this is my tone, copy it." It changes the outcome more than any other instruction.
Always finish by asking two things: "what's NOT included" and "what more do you need to know to do this better." That's where the gaps that later cost money show up.
If the first attempt comes out generic, don't say "make it better": tell it exactly which line bothers you and why. "Cut this, it sounds like a brochure" works; "make it more natural" doesn't.
